scientific corroboration aims at truth-content elimination","Organisms do not 'choose' to be fit; scientists actively 'prefer' based on critical rules"],"overturn_conditions":["If biological evolution is shown to be teleological (aimed at truth)","If scientific theory choice is shown to be entirely random relative to test severity"],"shared_structure":["Selection based on survival of severe challenges","Preference for the variant with highest resilience so far","No guarantee of future survival despite past success"],"source_memory_refs":["biological_selection_process"],"transfer_claims":["Just as we expect the fittest organism to survive the next season without guarantee, we expect the best-corroborated theory to withstand the next test without logical necessity","The value lies in the rigor of the test survived, not the mere fact of survival"]},"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's own terms not as an inductive inference of future success, but as a non-justificationist 'critical choice' grounded in the methodological rule to prefer the theory with greater empirical content and severity of testing; however, accepting this defense costs the scientist any rational guarantee that the preferred theory will work in practice, reducing the preference to a bold conjecture about which error has been most thoroughly eliminated so far.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the preference implies any probability assignment >0.5 to the theory's future success, it violates Popper's anti-induction stance.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the mechanism cannot explain why a scientist should act on the corroborated theory rather than flipping a coin between unfalsified theories, it fails the pragmatic test.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'content' argument secretly relies on the uniformity of nature (that what worked before will work again), it smuggles in induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Critical Choice via Content Maximization: The mechanism distinguishes between 'justification' (which requires induction) and 'choice' (which relies on comparing logical content and test severity). A scientist prefers Theory B over Theory A not because B is more likely true, but because B has survived tests that would have falsified A, meaning B contains more information about the world. The 'cost' is the admission that this preference offers no security against future falsification; it is a decision to bet on the theory that has told us more, acknowledging that it might still be wrong tomorrow.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
